relations.note: Later summaries and reconstructions sometimes call Laima the daughter of Dievs.

relations.myth: Divine transport in celestial wedding arrangements
relations.note: Variants associate Dievs’s horses and Laima’s wagon with wedding arrangements.
Dievs and Laima travel, deliberate, bless, or oversee human fate together.
Laima embodies fate alongside Dievs as spiritual or cosmic order.
Later interpretations infer that Perkūnas is Dievas’s son from Dievaitis and Christianized folklore.
Christianized folklore makes Pērkons an agent who carries out the high God’s punishments.

relations.myth: Celestial wedding and striking the golden oak
relations.note: Pērkons joins or disrupts wedding cycles involving Dievs’s sons.
Latvian songs place Dievs and Pērkons together in a divine dance.

relations.myth: Celestial wedding and neighboring heavenly households
relations.note: Their heavenly households are allied through his sons’ courtship of Saule’s daughters.
Saule attends Dievs’s feast or participates in his ordered celestial household.

relations.myth: God and Velnias create the world
relations.note: Velnias accompanies God, retrieves primordial earth, and shares creative labor.

relations.myth: God and Devil create the world
relations.note: They form land, animals, or terrain while Velns imitates or sabotages Dievs.

relations.myth: Opposed creation of animals and landscape
relations.note: Velnias imitates God’s creations, producing harmful creatures and uneven or barren terrain.
Velnias hides some retrieved earth in his mouth, attempting to appropriate it from God.

relations.myth: God and Devil travel among humans
relations.note: They travel together as opposing figures testing hospitality, greed, and disorder.
God and Žemyna jointly receive offerings and appear together in prayers.
Laima occasionally appears in formulas concerning the Sun’s allotted day, without a stable narrative relationship.
Saule and Laima jointly appear in songs of fate, birth, marriage, and women’s lives.
Laima admits the child into life while the earth mother receives the dead.
After Pērkons strikes the celestial tree, Saulė mourns or gathers its golden branches.
Perkūnas avenges Moon’s love of Aušrinė by splitting him with a sword.
Pērkons appears in variants involving disrupted weddings, damaged celestial trees, or punishment.

relations.myth: Perkūnas pursues the hiding devil during thunderstorms
relations.note: Perkūnas attacks Velnias with lightning as he hides in natural objects, animals, or people.
Velnias hides in stones, trees, water, animals, or clothing while Perkūnas attacks.
relations.source: Lithuanian belief legends published by Vėlius

relations.note: Latvian folklore associates thunder with Pērkons pursuing Velns or another evil being.
Modern synthetic accounts pair Perkūnas with the earth goddess Žemyna; no early source confirms the marriage.
Modern scholarship and revival tradition pair him with Žemyna as a fertilizing counterpart.
Popular modern genealogies allege that Žemyna is Saulė's daughter.

Andajus.myth: Gods worshipped by Mindaugas and Lithuanians
Andajus.note: Andajus and Perkūnas appear in the same Lithuanian divine list without narrative interaction.

Auseklis.note: Auseklis courts or joins the wedding of a Saules meita.

Austėja.note: Łasicki lists both goddesses together and says they assist growth.

Auxtheias Vissagistis.note: Later interpreters equated Łasicki’s highest Samogitian god with Dievas.

Aušrinė.note: Greimas reconstructs Laimė as Aušrinė’s godmother and birth-and-fate deity.

Aušrinė.myth: Perkūnas strikes the celestial wedding tree
Aušrinė.note: Perkūnas strikes a tree in a celestial-wedding song associated with Aušrinė.
Aušrinė becomes Saulė’s rival when the estranged Moon loves her.
Some Lithuanian traditions describe Aušrinė as Saulė’s daughter.
Aušrinė serves Saulė in the morning and prepares her way.
Modern reconstructions claim Velnias abducts or possesses Aušrinė, provoking the thunder-god’s pursuit.

Christ.note: Christ or a wandering divine figure defeats, exposes, or corrects Velnias.

Christian God.note: Christian translators adopted Dievas, Dievs, and Deiws as the ordinary name for God.

Christian saints.note: Saints and their holy names or signs repel Velnias in Christianized legends.

Dalia.note: Laima and Dalia overlap as allotter and allotted share, forming the compound Laima-Dalia.

Dieva dēli.note: Latvian songs repeatedly identify the divine horsemen as Dievs’s sons.
The sons of Dievs row a golden boat to assist or rescue Saule.
The sons of Dievs court Saule’s daughters in celestial-wedding songs.

Dēkla.note: They care for infants and allot life, occasionally coordinating or occupying parallel song lines.
Modern writers arrange Laima, Dēkla, and Kārta as three fate-goddess sisters.

Earth.myth: Sun and Moon care for Earth
Earth.note: Some variants call Earth their child, watched alternately by Sun and Moon.

Giltinė.note: Laima allots life or fortune while Giltinė brings death; some narratives place both beside a newborn.

Holy Angel.note: Žemyna's prayer invokes an angel to stand nearby and repel harmful people.

Kapu māte.note: Laima’s life-allotting role contrasts with the grave mother’s reception of the dead.
Different song variants assign the grave key to either earth or grave mother.

Kārta.note: Both determine or hang a person’s course; Kārta may specialize the concept of fate.
Modern writers arrange Laima, Dēkla, and Kārta as three fate-goddess sisters.

Laimė.note: Žemyna and Laimė could be invoked together during childbirth ceremonies.

Laumė.note: Overlapping childbirth, spinning, and fate functions caused disputed identification through Praetorius’s spelling Leumele.
Regional folklore sometimes links Perkūnas matrimonially with Laumė or a female atmospheric being.

Mary.note: Mary’s holy name, signs, or prayers drive Velnias away in folk-Christian belief.

Māra.myth: Beneficent invocation with Māra and Laima
Māra.note: Traditional formulas jointly invoke Dievs, Māra, and Laima as beneficent powers.
Dievturi theology and art coordinate Dievs with Māra and Laima.
They attend childbirth, women, cattle, and household welfare, sometimes appearing together or substituting for one another.
Laima represents fate while Māra represents material manifestation.
Some variants attach Māra’s handling or advice about bloody garments to the heavenly-tree episode.
Some Latvian scholarship and Dievturi theology merge Māra's earthly domain with Zemes māte.

Mēness.myth: Wedding of Dievs’s sons and Saule’s daughters
Mēness.note: Mēness exchanges rings during the celestial wedding involving Dievs’s sons.
Latvian variants inconsistently cast Mēness as Saule’s spouse or wedding partner.

Mėnulis.note: Moon marries Saulė, separates from her, and later loves Aušrinė.
Lithuanian belief texts alternatively describe Sun and Moon as siblings.
Sun and Moon quarrel over dividing or alternating care of Earth.
Popular modern genealogies allege that Žemyna is Mėnulis's daughter.

Ockopirmus.note: Later scholars identified the Sudovian chief god of sky and stars with Dievas.

Patollo.myth: Three gods appear at the sacred oak
Patollo.note: Grunau places Perkuno and Patollo together in an embellished Prussian divine triad.
Later reconstruction identifies Grunau’s death-associated Patollo as an Old Prussian Velnias equivalent.

Peckols.note: Modern authors equate this Old Prussian underworld-associated figure with Velnias.

Potrimpo.myth: Three gods appear at the sacred oak
Potrimpo.note: Grunau places Perkuno and Potrimpo together in an embellished Prussian divine triad.

Prakorimas.note: Later interpreters equated Stryjkowski’s disputed creator or highest deity with Dievas.

Saules meita.myth: Pērkons disrupts the Sun daughter’s wedding
Saules meita.note: Celestial-wedding variants make Pērkons oppose or disrupt the wedding party involving Saules meita.
One song variant asks Saules meita instead of Zemes māte for the key.

Saules meitas.note: Saule mothers and cares for one or several Sun-daughters.

Teliavelis.myth: Gods worshipped by Mindaugas and Lithuanians
Teliavelis.note: Teliavelis and Perkūnas appear in the same Lithuanian divine list without narrative interaction.
The mighty smith Teliavelis forges the Sun.
Greimas connected Velnias with the medieval divine smith Teliavelis, without textual identification.

Vakarinė.note: Vakarinė prepares Saulė’s bed or receives her at day’s end.
Some modern genealogical syntheses describe Vakarinė as Saulė’s daughter.

Veļu māte.note: Laima hangs or gives the cradle; Veļu māte removes it and receives the dead.
Latvian songs alternate them as receivers or guardians of the dead.

Vielona.note: Later scholarship disputes whether Łasicki’s god of souls Vielona is Velnias.

Virgin Mary.note: Christian Mary assumes or shares Laima’s protection of childbirth in charms and belief texts.
Mary appears as an additional or alternate patron where Žemyna receives libation.

angels.note: Christianized birth-fate variants place angels within episodes otherwise centered on Laima or fate women.

the stars.note: Late folklore and scholarly syntheses sometimes make Sun and Moon parents of the stars.

the zodiacal signs.note: The signs shatter the Sun’s prison tower with a great hammer.

Žemėpatis.note: Prätorius classifies Žemyna as the sister of Žemėpatis.

Žvorūna.myth: Gods worshipped by Mindaugas and Lithuanians
Žvorūna.note: Žvorūna and Perkūnas appear in the same Lithuanian divine list without narrative interaction.
